title: The lost book (2 Kings 22)
hook: workmen find the law in the temple, and young King Josiah tears his clothes
carry: the book was lost in the house

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dothan and a prayer for sight, and your line was more with us.

A renovation is under way in the temple in Jerusalem. Carpenters, builders and masons are at work, and money for timber and hewn stone is being counted out. The king is Josiah. The text says he became king at eight years old, and this is the eighteenth year of his reign. In the middle of the work, the high priest Hilkiah sends word to the king's scribe, Shaphan, in one plain sentence: "I have found the book of the law in the house of the LORD." Found. In the house of the Lord, where you'd think it should never have gone missing.
screen: `I HAVE FOUND THE BOOK OF THE LAW.`

segments.voice: Shaphan reads it to himself, then carries it to the king and reads it aloud, and the text says: "when the king had heard the words of the book of the law, that he rent his clothes." Words that were in his own temple the whole time. The text never says how the book went missing. No theft, no fire. Some readers picture it lost the quiet way things get lost in a busy house: under other things, while everyone was occupied with the building. Then Josiah does something interesting. He doesn't ask the priests to explain it. He sends them to enquire of the Lord, and they go to a prophet, a woman named Huldah, who lives in Jerusalem. Her answer is hard news for the city, but for the king there's a tender line: "Because thine heart was tender, and thou hast humbled thyself before the LORD." What saves the moment isn't that Josiah already knew. It's that, hearing it late, he let it reach him. In the next chapter he gathers everyone, small and great, and reads the whole book to them himself. Which book was it? The chapter calls it the book of the law and doesn't say more; some readers connect it with Deuteronomy. Either way, the story puts the loss somewhere uncomfortable: not out in the world, but inside the house of worship, among people working hard on the building.

Let your mind walk through your rooms and find a book you've let gather dust, a Bible, a letter, a journal, or a word someone once said to you that you've stopped rereading. Don't scold yourself; Josiah wasn't the one who lost it, and he still let it reach him. Picture picking it up, and if you pray, hold it before God for a moment; if you don't, just hold it, and let it be found.
Josiah. The young king who heard the book of the law, found in the temple during repairs, and tore his clothes.
Your line: the book was lost in the house. And it was found there too. Day seven hundred thirty-eight, done.

howItsDone: Some Christians mark a return to Bible reading by remembering Josiah's discovery, and churches sometimes use 2 Kings 22 to encourage people to read scripture for themselves and aloud together.

chat.says: Why did King Josiah tear his clothes when the old book was read?
options: He heard words lost in his own temple, and let them reach his heart.
He was angry the priests had hidden the book from him on purpose.
Tearing clothes was how kings showed a new law was now in force.
chat.meaning: The book of the law turned up during temple repairs. Hearing it late, Josiah let it reach him, and Huldah said his heart was tender.

Hilkiah.meaning: the high priest who found the book of the law

Shaphan.meaning: the king's scribe, who read the book to Josiah

Huldah.meaning: a prophet in Jerusalem whom the king's men consulted

Deuteronomy.meaning: a book of the Bible some readers link to the found book

notes: Josiah's age (eight) and 'the eighteenth year' are from 2 Kings 22:1 and 22:3.
'Tearing your clothes is what people in these stories do at a death' is a general observation (e.g. 2 Samuel 1:11, 3:31); confirm phrasing.
Spoken quotation of 22:19 is to the king via Huldah; the KJV verse is 'Because thine heart was tender, and thou hast humbled thyself before the LORD, when thou heardest...'. Partial quote.
The Deuteronomy identification is attributed to 'some readers' only; confirm the Keeper is happy to mention it.
